name: Pennsylvania Bank House

revival_periods.note: Revived weakly and mostly as an aesthetic — fieldstone with an exposed lower level on a sloping lot — rather than as the working refrigeration strategy it was.

regions: Lancaster, Berks, Lebanon and Montgomery counties, Pennsylvania
geography.hearth: the rolling limestone country of the Pennsylvania German counties, where cross-slopes of one in six to one in ten are the normal condition of a farm site

lineage.note: The Alpine and Rhenish habit of setting a house across a slope so that the byre or cellar opens at the lower grade arrives with the Palatine and Swiss migration and is applied here to a dwelling rather than a farm building.

description.short: A Pennsylvania German stone house set across a hillside so that its lower storey opens at grade on the downhill side and is buried on the uphill side, giving a cool service level and two front doors at two different levels.
description.long:
The bank house is the most literal piece of environmental engineering in colonial American domestic building, and it is almost entirely invisible from the uphill approach. Set a house across a slope of one in six or steeper. Cut into the hill on the upper side and build the lower storey against the cut, so that three of its walls are surrounded by earth and only the downhill wall sees daylight. That lower storey is now a room that will not freeze in January and will not exceed the mid fifties in August. Put the kitchen, the dairy, the root store and the meat there. If the site has a spring — and the limestone country is full of them — build directly over it so that the water runs across the floor and out through an arched opening in the downhill wall, and you have running cold water and a dairy at fifty degrees, permanently, for the cost of moving earth.

The consequences run right through the building. There are two front doors on two different levels: one entering the lower service storey from the downhill grade, one entering the Stube level from the upper grade, sometimes across a short bridge or a stone stoop. The uphill elevation is one storey shorter than the downhill one, so the same house presents two entirely different faces. The uphill wall carries earth pressure and therefore has few openings or none. And because the lower level is doing the work of a cellar without being underground, the principal floor above it is dry — a serious matter in a period when the alternative was a damp cellar under a damp floor.

The rest is standard Pennsylvania German: eighteen to thirty inches of squared limestone or sandstone with oversized quoins, a steep forty-five to fifty degree roof framed with a liegender Stuhl leaning truss, small irregular windows placed for the rooms behind them, a pent roof across the facade at the second-floor line, and a central chimney serving an open kitchen hearth on one side and a closed jamb stove on the other. Later examples regularize the front to five bays under Anglo pressure while keeping the section entirely unchanged, which is the standard fate of every immigrant tradition here.

To arrive at one from above is to see a modest one-and-a-half-storey stone cottage. To walk around it and look back from the field below is to see a three-storey stone wall with a spring running out of it. That gap between the two readings is the pleasure of the type, and it is also the reason it is under-recognized: half the building is a fact about the ground.

defining_characteristics: Sited across a slope so that the lowest storey is fully exposed on the downhill elevation and earth-bermed on the uphill elevation
Two principal entrances at two different grades — one to the service level, one to the living level — of unequal architectural status
Lower storey of 18–30 in squared stone housing kitchen, dairy and cold storage, frequently built over a spring discharging through an arched opening
Barrel-vaulted or heavy-beamed masonry ceiling over the lower storey
Uphill elevation with few or no openings; downhill elevation a full storey taller than the uphill one
Steep gable roof, 45–50 degrees, on a liegender Stuhl leaning-post truss over a usable loft
Central chimney serving an open hearth in the service level or kitchen and a closed jamb stove in the Stube above or alongside
diagnostic_tells: Two front doors at two different levels on two different elevations — decisive, and visible from a passing road
An arched opening at the base of the downhill wall with water running out of it
The uphill gable shows a one-and-a-half-storey house; the downhill gable shows two-and-a-half
No basement windows on the uphill side, and often no openings at all in that wall below the first floor
A pent roof band across the facade with no posts beneath it

distinguished_from.difference: The parent style covers both banked and level-sited houses. This variant is specifically the banked case, and it is worth separating because the section, the door count, the circulation and the room programme all change when the house is set into a hill.

A Georgian house on a slope gets an exposed English basement and keeps one front door on the piano nobile, entered up a flight of steps, with symmetrical windows above. The bank house gets two doors of equal practical importance, an asymmetric plan, unaligned windows and no ceremonial approach at all.

The revival 'Pennsylvania farmhouse' on a sloping lot exposes a walkout basement with a garage in it, keeps a symmetrical five-bay front with a centred classical door, and uses four inches of veneer stone. The bank house has two feet of load-bearing masonry, a vaulted service ceiling and no ceremonial entrance.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The slope sets the section: the fall across the building footprint must equal roughly one storey height (7–9 ft) for the type to work at all.
typical_ratios: Cross-slope 1:6 to 1:10 across the building depth; total fall 6–10 ft across 22–30 ft
Lower-storey wall 22–30 in; upper storey 18–24 in
Lower-storey ceiling 6 ft 6 in – 7 ft 6 in; principal floor 7 ft 6 in – 8 ft 6 in
Pent roof projection 30–42 in at the second-floor line, pitch 25–35 degrees
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Irregular and driven by the plan; a nominal three- or five-bay front emerges after about 1790 but rarely aligns floor to floor.

massing_affinities.note: The nearest catalogued skeleton to the banked Flurküchenhaus.
Small tenant bank houses of a single room per level.
Growth along the contour with a summer-kitchen wing.

constraints.statement: Requires a cross-slope of at least 1:8 (12.5%) across the building depth, giving a fall of not less than 6 ft. On a level site the type cannot exist; a house with a walkout basement on flat ground is not a bank house.

test.note: 1:8. The fall figure (not less than 6ft) restates the same requirement over the building's actual depth and stays prose.

constraints.statement: The lower-storey finished floor sits within 12 in of the downhill grade at the exposed wall, and the uphill wall is bermed to within 12 in of the principal floor level. Lower-storey walls not less than 22 in of load-bearing stone to carry earth pressure.

test.note: Tests the lower-storey wall thickness, the cleanest single claim in a compound statement. The two grade-relationship clauses (finished floor within 12in of downhill grade; uphill wall bermed within 12in of principal floor) stay prose.

constraints.statement: Two exterior doors at two levels, on different elevations. A single ceremonial entrance destroys the type: the service level must be enterable without passing through the house.
No openings in the bermed (uphill) wall below the principal floor. Where a spring is captured, the discharge is through an arched opening 18–30 in wide at the base of the downhill wall.
Roof pitch 12:12 to 14:12; pent roof, where used, projects 30–42 in at the second-floor line, unposted, returning 12–24 in at the corners.

test.note: The pent roof clause restates the same feature already tested on german-pennsylvania-colonial and stays prose here.

exemplars.name: Heinrich Zeller House (Fort Zeller)
exemplars.note: Limestone house built into a bank over an everflowing spring that discharges from an arched opening in the basement; narrow irregularly placed windows, steep gable, central twelve-foot fireplace.
exemplars.why: The spring runs from the bedrock through the basement and out of an arched opening, which is this node's whole argument in one building -- on Wikipedia's account, which is where the record's banking claim comes from. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026 by the cluster audit: this why had said the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission's field guide 'reaches for' this building when it explains the banked house. It does not. The PHMC entry describes banked houses in a paragraph that names no building at all, and names Fort Zeller in a separate paragraph on FORTIFIED houses -- 'was not actually a fort but such a fortified (thick walled) house built in this manner'. The record's own ref note says so; the why did not.

exemplars.name: Schifferstadt
exemplars.note: Built by Elias Bruner of the Palatinate; central wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl truss, vaulted cellar and five-plate jamb stove all survive, making the section unusually legible.
exemplars.why: A National Historic Landmark whose section survives entire - wishbone chimney, liegender Stuhl, vaulted cellar, jamb stove - so the node's figures for the service level can be held against something documented rather than described.

exemplars.name: Furnace Hills Tenant House
exemplars.location: West Cocalico Township, Lancaster County, Pennsylvania
exemplars.note: A 19th-century banked sandstone dwelling of about 19 by 26 ft, explicitly documented as a vernacular Pennsylvania German perpendicular bank house — the modest end of the type.
exemplars.why: The National Register itself types this building 'Penn. German Bankhouse', and at 19 by 26 ft it is the plainest measurable instance the corpus has; it is also the only one that banks its GABLE end into the ground, which this node's description does not distinguish.

exemplars.name: Jonathan Hager House
exemplars.location: 110 Key Street, Hagerstown City Park, Washington County, Maryland
exemplars.note: A fieldstone house of about 1740 built over two springs that join in the cellar, whose bottom floor is three rooms - two of them containing the springs, one with an enormous fireplace and serving as the principal kitchen - under a near-central brick chimney rising from a limestone hearth on the ground floor. HABS states the section in one line: 'Two and one-half above cellar, which is banked on one side.'
exemplars.why: The only building in this node whose banked section is stated in those words by a federal surveyor rather than inferred, and the same sheet argues the spring from dairy and cold storage rather than from defence - which is this node's own reasoning, reached independently in about 1940.

exemplars.name: Hupp House
exemplars.note: A rubble limestone dwelling of about 1755 on a banked site, 20 ft wide by 40 ft deep, with a traditional Germanic central chimney and a steep gable roof. The 1995 Virginia county survey calls it three storeys with the two lower built into a steep bank above a spring-fed pool, records a spring trough channelling water across the cellar floor, and notes that 'The present upper cellar was originally the principal floor of the house and served as the kuche'. Wikipedia says four storeys; both are recorded.
exemplars.why: The Shenandoah Valley is one of this node's own named regions and had no exemplar; this is 'one of the oldest extant dwellings erected by Germanic settlers in Shenandoah County' on WIKIPEDIA's account, and its principal floor has become a cellar -- 'The present upper cellar was originally the principal floor of the house and served as the kuche' -- which is the 1995 Virginia Department of Historic Resources county survey's own sentence and the clearest statement anywhere of what banking does to a section. CORRECTED 5 Sep 2026: the age claim had been attributed to the Department, whose own file 085-0007 states only the date and the presumed builder.

sources: Sally McMurry and Nancy Van Dolsen, eds., Architecture and Landscape of the Pennsylvania Germans, 1720–1920 (2011)
Robert F. Ensminger, The Pennsylvania Barn: Its Origin, Evolution, and Distribution in North America (2nd ed., 2003)
Bernard L. Herman and Gabrielle Lanier, Everyday Architecture of the Mid-Atlantic (1997)
Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, Pennsylvania Architectural Field Guide: Pennsylvania German Traditional, 1700–1870

proportion_packs.note: Secondary, behind `brick-course`, and the pair on this node is the useful thing rather than either alone. A bank house is built into a slope with a masonry ground storey and a lighter one above, and the two packs divide on that line: this one holds the heavy stone below, `brick-course` the work above where it is brick. The pack's plinth rule is doing unusual work here, because on a bank house the lower wall is a retaining wall for part of its length and the splash line the plinth answers is on one elevation and not the others.

Inherits the parent style's stone construction directly and is explicitly named in brick-course's own applies_to. The lower (banked) storey wall is specified at not less than 22 in of load-bearing stone to carry earth pressure — the pack's reveal_masonry rule (wall thickness in whole wythes) applies exactly, and its window_head_masonry segmental/flat-arch rules govern the few, deliberately placed openings in the exposed downhill wall.

pennsylvania-bank-house is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The banked plan is, if anything, more function-constrained than the parent's: room size follows the slope, the spring and the stove wall, never a ratio.

Bound cautiously, as an analogy rather than a direct fit. storey-graduation's own 'GROUND STOREY UNDER A PIANO NOBILE' rule (a markedly lower storey below the principal floor, ratio about 0.72) describes the same geometric shape this variant's own typical_ratios record — a lower-storey ceiling of 6'6"-7'6" against a principal floor of 7'6"-8'6" — even though the reason for the height difference is entirely different: the pack's rule is about architectural hierarchy under a piano nobile, while the bank house's lower storey is a working refrigeration cellar set by the cross-slope, not by design ambition. The ratio is offered as a usable starting point for the section, not as evidence the two traditions share a rationale. No pack among the 36 models hillside/bank siting directly, which is the more honest statement of this variant's real governing geometry.
